captions.instagram:
How does a synthesizer work?

A synthesizer builds sound from nothing but electricity: oscillators hum, a filter carves, an envelope shapes every note. Play a real synth in your browser, take a Minimoog-style keyboard apart in 3D, and see why two sine waves can ring like a bell.

→ A synthesizer makes sound from electricity: oscillators, a filter, an amplifier, and keys to play them.
→ Early synths were modular: separate boxes joined by patch cables in any order you like.
→ Every tone is a stack of sine waves. Add harmonics one by one and a sine turns into a sawtooth.
→ A square wave uses only odd harmonics. A triangle’s fade much faster, so it sounds soft.
→ A filter carves harmonics away. Sweep its cutoff down and the bright buzz turns dark: the classic wah.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/synthclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: How does a synthesizer work? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
A synthesizer builds sound from nothing but electricity: oscillators hum, a filter carves, an envelope shapes every note. Play a real synth in your browser, take a Minimoog-style keyboard apart in 3D, and see why two sine waves can ring like a bell.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox-production-fd52.up.railway.app/e/synthclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/synthclear

In this video:
• Oscillators, a filter, an amplifier. A classic synth has three main parts in a row.
• Every tone is a stack of sine waves. Any repeating wave is a sum of sine waves at 1, 2, 3… times its frequency: its harmonics.
• Subtractive: start bright, carve away. A lowpass filter lets low frequencies through and cuts the high harmonics.
• Attack, decay, sustain, release. An envelope gives each note a shape in time.
• FM: one wave wobbles another. John Chowning found at Stanford that wobbling a sine wave's frequency very fast adds sidebands at the carrier plus and minus multiples of the modulator.
• MIDI: messages, not sound. Since 1983, instruments talk in MIDI: three bytes such as note on, which note, and how hard, sent at 31,250 bits a second.

Glassbox opens one box a day: an interactive model of how something works, plus the code behind it.
